Discuss personal online habits with a partner, using vocabulary from the unit (e.g., "I watch TV shows and music videos online every day").
Practice conversations about health problems, using phrases like "I burned my hand yesterday" or "You should see a doctor."
Talk about fitness, health, healthy and unhealthy habits identifying and reflecting on their habits and classifying them.

skills.listening: The learner understands clear, standard English on topics like family, school, routines, endangered animals, online activities, and health. They follow simple instructions, identify activities, verify statements, and recognize time phrases in spoken texts. The learner will engage with conversations and videos about weekend activities and transportation.
skills.reading: The learner reads short texts with familiar vocabulary, adeptly locating details, guessing new word meanings, skimming, sequencing events, and matching problems to solutions in contexts like food, parties, and habitats. The learner will analyze e-mails, social media posts, and travel blogs about weekend plans and travel experiences.
skills.speaking: The learner articulates clear sentences about themselves, places, and preferences, discussing online habits, health, and advice (e.g., “You should rest”) with minimal errors, though occasional hesitation may occur. The learner will converse about weekend plans, transportation, and travel, using structures like “What are you doing this weekend?” to make arrangements, and compare transport modes. /
skills.vocabulary: The learner commands a robust vocabulary for family, food, animals, online activities, and health. The learner will acquire vocabulary for weekend activities (e.g., sleepover, cookout), phrasal verbs of movement (e.g., “take off,” “pick up”), transportation (e.g., ferry, subway), and travel adjectives.
skills.grammar: The learner proficiently uses present simple, present continuous, “there is/there are,” “there was/there were,” simple past, and “should/shouldn’t” for advice, forming accurate sentences and questions. The learner will master the present progressive for future plans (e.g., “I’m seeing my cousin tonight”), indefinite pronouns (e.g., someone, anywhere) in various sentence types, and comparative adjectives.

items: Students learn to discuss and describe their weekend activities and plans using appropriate vocabulary and grammar structures.
Students practice using phrasal verbs related to movement, such as "take off," "get on," "go away," "get back," "go out," and "pick up".
Students develop skills to make plans and arrangements with others, using conversational structures like "What are you doing this weekend?" and "Do you want to hang out?”
Students learn to use the present progressive tense to talk about future plans (e.g., "I’m seeing my cousin tonight") and practice affirmative, negative, and question forms.

Students master the use of indefinite pronouns (e.g., someone, something, somewhere, anyone, anything, anywhere, no one, nothing, nowhere, everyone, everything, everywhere) in affirmative, negative, and question sentences
Students practice using comparative adjectives (short, long, and irregular) to compare transportation methods, vehicles, or travel experiences (e.g., "The bus is easier than the subway")
Students describe travel experiences, including trips and vacations. Students use travel-related vocabulary (e.g., crowded, traditional, modern, historic) to describe destinations and experiences.

skills.listening: The learner may be able to understand very basic spoken English, such as greetings, or some objects that are around them, but they are unable to comprehend sentences in English and struggle to decode the language.
skills.reading: The learner gets confused when they are trying to read and they are unfamiliar with some sounds or clusters which may affect their reading fluency.
skills.speaking: The learner can say single words or very short phrases. They hesitate to speak, have a very limited vocabulary, and find pronunciation difficult. Most of the answers in this level are in their mother tongue.
skills.vocabulary: The learner might identify some vocabulary related to things around them, but still their vocabulary range is very limited and it affects their understanding of the language.
skills.grammar: The learner mostly uses words and not sentences. They might use some phrases but they make mistakes and are inconsistent. They need to learn about the parts of speech and start making sentences. /

Practice short phrases to share personal information (e.g., "I am 8," "I like to play").
Begin to introduce themselves (e.g., "My name is…") in guided, teacher-led activities.

skills.listening: The learner is able to understand simple spoken English in familiar contexts, such as classroom instructions (e.g., "Listen and repeat," "Write your name"). They can comprehend very short sentences about routine and school related topics.
skills.reading: The learner can understand and read short, simple texts with familiar words, especially about personal topics like school or basic information. They also use visuals, titles, or teacher help to make sense of what they’re reading.
skills.speaking: The learner uses basic vocabulary to form simple sentences, join guided conversations with practiced phrases, and talk about familiar topics like school or hobbies.
skills.vocabulary: The learner understands and uses basic, high-frequency words about school, daily life, and personal info in simple sentences, but may mix up similar words or forget new ones without repetition. Their vocab is limited to familiar contexts.
skills.grammar: The learner uses basic grammar to allow them to make very short sentences like with (verb to be) in the present simple. They can complete guided tasks but still make common mistakes with verb forms and word order. /

items: Expand vocabulary to include basic descriptors, bedroom vocabulary, places around the city ability and interest vocabulary.
Use "This is…" and simple present tense (e.g., "It is…") through repetition and imitation.
Share abilities (e.g., "I can swim") and asking peers (e.g., "Can you dance?").
Practice short phrases to share abilities (e.g., "I can swim," "I can jump").
Answer simple questions with one-word or yes/no responses (e.g., "Can you sing? Yes").
Describe their bedroom and what it has in short sentences.

skills.listening: The learner understands simple spoken English in familiar settings, like classroom instructions (e.g., "Listen and repeat") or short sentences about routines, school, bedrooms, or abilities (e.g., "I can dance"). They grasp basic phrases about city places (e.g., "This is a shop") with repetition and clear context.
skills.reading: The learner reads short, simple texts with familiar words about school, daily life, bedrooms, or city places. They use visuals or teacher help to understand and recognize basic descriptors (e.g., "big," "small") and ability words (e.g., "swim," "jump") in guided tasks.
skills.speaking: The learner forms simple sentences using basic vocabulary to talk about school, hobbies, bedrooms, or abilities. They share abilities, ask peers questions , and give one-word or yes/no answers. They describe their bedroom briefly. /
skills.vocabulary: The learner uses high-frequency words for school, daily life, bedrooms, city places, abilities, and descriptors. They may mix up similar words or forget new ones without practice, sticking to familiar contexts.
skills.grammar: The learner uses basic grammar, like present simple "to be" and "can" for abilities. They mimic structures like "This is…" in guided tasks but often make mistakes with verb forms or word order when using the language.

items: Develop skills to understand and provide simple instructions using imperatives.
Learn phrases and structures to ask for items in a shopping context (e.g., "Do you have any laptops?").
Use the simple present tense to describe daily routines (e.g., "I get up at 6:45," "She goes to school at 8:00").
Learn vocabulary related to daily activities (e.g., "have breakfast," "do homework," "go to bed").
Talk about a favorite day, including activities, times, and locations (e.g., "On Saturday, I play soccer in the afternoon").
Use time phrases (e.g., "in the morning," "at three o’clock") to structure descriptions.
Build vocabulary for daily routines, chores, possessions, and time expressions.

skills.listening: The learner comprehends simple spoken English in familiar contexts like following classroom instructions and understanding short sentences about routines, abilities, city places, imperatives and shopping. They need to improve their listening through expanding the topics they are familiar with like celebrities’ style and videos about markets, engaging with real-world contexts.
skills.reading: The learner reads simple texts with familiar vocabulary and is ready to expand their comprehension  through enhancing their understanding of habits (healthy and unhealthy ones), clothes, and personal style.
skills.speaking: The learner can use very short sentences to discuss school, hobbies, and abilities and describe routines or a favorite day using time phrases.They may make mistakes or struggle with fluency. They will talk about good and bad habits, food preferences, and people’s appearance and clothing, gaining confidence in detailed descriptions. /
skills.vocabulary: They have limited vocabulary and cover things they are familiar with like vocabulary about school, daily life, abilities, and time expressions from, though they may confuse similar terms. They will learn words related to habits, clothes, and style, enabling richer discussions about routines and preferences.
skills.grammar: They can use very basic grammar to talk about themselves and things around them. They use the simple present for routines, with occasional errors in verb forms. They will master adverbs of frequency (e.g., "always," "never") and form questions with question words to discuss daily life and preferences.

items: Learn to identify, describe, and categorize good and bad habits (e.g., being on time vs. forgetting gym clothes).
Students will engage in quizzes to assess their eating habits and compare answers.
Focus on daily routines and personal habits, using adverbs of frequency (e.g., always, sometimes, never) to describe how often activities occur.
Listen to conversations about celebrities (e.g., Selena Gomez) to understand descriptions of style and appearance.
Form questions using question words (e.g., What, Where, When) and the present simple tense to discuss personal preferences and routines.
Learn vocabulary related to habits, clothes, and personal style (e.g., boots, cap, dress).
Describe people’s appearance and clothing using learned vocabulary.
